Orthogonal Latin Squares

Number TheoryAlgorithmsLogic
Game: Every square holds a small letter and a capital. Arrange them so that each small letter and each capital appears once in every row and every column, and no pair of letters is repeated anywhere.
How to play: Press two squares in the same row to swap their small letters (or capitals), or press the arrows to slide a whole row or column around. Choose which letters move with “Apply to”.

Apply to
Look for the math

Two Latin squares of the same size are orthogonal if, laid on top of each other, every possible pair of letters appears exactly once. For size N there are N² cells and N² pairs, so “no pair twice” means “every pair once”.

Counting

The test counted every Latin square of size 2 to 5: there are 2, 12, 576 and 161,280. Pairing every square of size 2, 3 and 4 with every other gave 0, 72 and 6,912 orthogonal pairs. So there are none of size 2 at all, and 72 of size 3 (a cyclic pair is one of them).

Building them

For an odd size N take the squares i + j and i + 2j (mod N): both are Latin because 2 has an inverse, and a pair of cells with the same two letters would have the same i + j and i + 2j, so the same j and the same i. For sizes 4, 8 and 16, work in the field with that many elements. For sizes like 12 or 20, multiply a pair of size 4 by a pair of odd size. The button shows such a pair for every size from 3 to 20 that these cover, and the test checked each of them.

Euler's 36 officers

Which sizes have an orthogonal pair? Euler guessed that none of the sizes 2, 6, 10, 14, ... (twice an odd number) do. He was right for 2 and for 6: Gaston Tarry showed in 1900 by hand that six regiments of six ranks cannot be arranged, so nobody can win with a 6 by 6 board. But in 1959–60 Bose, Shrikhande and Parker built pairs for 10, 14, 18 and every larger size of this form. So the only sizes without a pair are 2 and 6. (The test checked the claim for 2 directly; the case 6 is Tarry's theorem and was not re-checked here, and the page does not build pairs for 10, 14 and 18.)

A note on the applet

The original applet announced success after comparing each cell only with cells below and to its right. That misses pairs of cells that sit on the other diagonal, and for size 4 it would accept 18,432 pairs of Latin squares though only 6,912 are orthogonal. This version compares every pair of cells.

Press “Show a solution” for size 5, then spoil it with a swap and try to repair it. The cells that repeat a pair of letters are outlined in red.
